The recent meteor in Siberia came close as a warning, and this time it got world publicity unlike the one about a century ago. Siberia is a big place so it's likely to 'win the lottery'. But yes, the warnings have been given.

Asteroid impacts and meteor impacts have occurred over and in populated areas.

It just didn't create a calamity or disaster with it.

I agree with the OP that this is a disaster threat that should be taken seriously.

The search for Near Earth Asteroids is only one part of the issue.

The bigger part of the issue is how much delta-V is required to intercept the object and then how do you deflect it sufficiently to change the impact probability. This issue alone requires a heavy-lift launch vehicle and delta-V.

Well, as with all things, this boils down to a Nature v Nurture debate. While evolved, yes, it's important to realize geographic/cultural area so you can form sort of a comparison. I'm of the thought that the environment has an effect on the actual biology, and neurology (something I don't quite have a firm grasp of). While humans are technically social creatures, you have to take into account population density, religious beliefs, and geography.

example: A person in a large city with limited to moderate exposure to a religious group might have more social interactions with peers and non familial friends, and might hate being "mothered" due to a large group of outside influences shaping their personality. That same person, if raised with a moderate to high exposure to a religious group might be more tolerant to overbearing familial tendencies.

A person In a rural area might have fewer social interactions with peers and non familial persons might rely ore heavily on their family social network, making them accustomed to "motherly" tendencies.

A person in a highly population dense are might have large social interations with non familial peers, but also due to lack of space, have to form close bonds with family making them more tolerant of motherly tendencies.

Now, it also depends on social construct. I have seen certain religious parents maintain control over children long after they've left the "nest" so to speak, and those individuals accept it as a way of life and treat their children the same.

There are advantages to both types of groups (I guess...), but I prefer the individualism and independence side.

I was a liberal adjunct professor. My liberal students didnt scare me at all.

She reasserts the idea that Professors taking safe stances because of fear of their jobs is real, along with claiming that students being empowered to professionally hurt professors they disagree with is a problem (concluding paragraph). This strikes me as a Professor whose only true problem with the article she is rebutting is the attitude and not the positions. I will agree with her that the demmand verse supply of Professors and people (like Scott Walker) who claim teachers who have it too good are a problem as well and make for a bad teaching atmosphere. This leaves me entirely unconvinced that identity politics isn't doing anti intellectual harm to academia though.

One thing the author did right though is focus on the problem being between the professors and academic institutions. Aside from that not much else.

Her points are: 1) I never had any complaints. 2) Students have always complained about her professors. It's the professors fault for self censoring and they have dysfunctional relationships with their universities. 3) You can't point to a real harm so you can't really claim anything is wrong.

1) I hate to be the guy that says it because discounting someone's experiences based on their sex is something I find extremely naive and ignorant: she is female. She is going to face less opposition from extremely liberal students when making her claims. The destructive call-out culture, identity politics etc is not directed at her. This is not to discredit her experiences however, and she does well to note that trigger warning requirements weren't something she had to deal with and may be hyperbole. Also the point that she makes that anecdotes do not make for evidence... is preceded with an anecdote.

2) Actually a decent point, however the problem here is that students wield lots of power and this identity politics craze and ultrasensitivity is threatening discourse. Yes it is due to this dysfunctional relationship between professor and institution but the one wielding the power granted by the university is the student body. Students are the judge and jury. Students have been granted this power by the institutions, professors have every reason to fear it as it is dictating how their jobs are performed.

3) The harm in this case is censored debate, fear of rocking the boat and turning academia into an echo chamber. Sure this is hard to quantify, but I'd love to see someone do so, perhaps in a rigorous survey of professors. I'd also like to see this level of scrutiny applied to identity politics too. Oh and did anyone else catch the irony about looking for 'real harm' when this is coming from identity politics?
